abstract: |
  A data analysis involves a sequence of decisions, from data cleaning to model specification, each of which can affect the reported result. Reproducing that result is not the same as understanding the sequence of decisions that produced it and the reasons for each: the code mixes those decisions with implementation details, while the manuscript states the major decisions and their rationale but scatters them across its sections and often leaves out the minor ones. A reader may then ask how the result would change under a different decision: the question itself is easy to pose, but implementing it is often non-trivial in practice. In this work, we propose a schema that represents a data analysis as a collection of decisions in natural language, from which large language models (LLMs) can generate and validate analysis scripts directly. This workflow can also expand a single analysis into a full multiverse of alternatives, specified in an alternative file, ready for comparison. We demonstrate the proposed workflow in two applications. In the first, we construct a schema for a published regression analysis of heaped smoking data and show that it reproduces the reported estimates, and that a reviewer-suggested alternative can be specified through the alternative file and turned into code automatically. In the second, where no schema is provided, we show how the workflow serves instead as a reproducibility check, applied to the many-analysts football study. As an intermediate representation between the manuscript and code scripts, our schema gives a self-contained account of an analysis and makes it extensible from a reader's perspective.
keywords:
  - Reproducibility
  - Large Language Models (LLMs)
  - Data analysis decisions
  - Many-analysts study
  - Statistical workflow
bibliography: bibliography.bib

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

<!-- , a gap also identified in prior work on authoring statistical models from conceptual relationships [@jun2022; @jun2022hypothesis].  -->

A data analysis is the product of a chain of decisions, from how the data are cleaned to how the model is specified. [This chain of decisions lets a reader comprehend the analysis, compare it against other analyses of similar questions, question how the result would change under an alternative decision.] Code and data availability, now standard reproducible practice [@peng_reproducible_2011; @wrobel_partnering_2024], guarantee that the reported result can be reproduced, [but not the chain of decisions that produced it.]

[Part of the reason is that] code and the decisions it implements operate at different levels: code specifies precisely what a computer should do, while a decision has a contextual interpretation that the code itself does not capture. Consider a line such as `dplyr::filter(df, x > 0)`, which has a precise meaning as code: keep rows where `x` is positive. Which decision this line encodes is not something the code can answer: it could represent restricting the analysis to a subpopulation for which $x > 0 $is substantively meaningful, or excluding observations flagged as invalid by anencoding convention where $x 
\le 0$ denotes missingness, and nothing in the `filter()` syntax indicates which is intended. Nor does code generally carry the rationale behind a decision, unless the author has left detailed comments. A better place to state the decisions is in the manuscript, where decisions are described along with their rationale. But this information is scattered across the manuscript rather than collected in one place, with preprocessing and modelling decisions appearing in different sections of the manuscript. Authors may also simply leave out decisions they consider minor, on the assumption that the code provides all the detail a reader would need. Reconstructing the full sequence, therefore, means searching across the paper and the code for decisions and their rationale before a reader can begin to comprehend the analysis. Ideally, this sequence of decisions and their rationale would live in a single file, so a reader can follow the analysis directly rather than piecing it together from multiple sources. This file should also be extensible, so a reader can specify an alternative decision and easily evaluate it to see how the result would change.

<!-- In other words, code and manuscript are complementary but each incomplete: the code is precise but mingled with implementation details and largely silent on rationale, while the manuscript carries rationale but scatters it across sections and sometimes omits it.  -->

<!-- What is needed is a representation that records each decision together with its rationale, in one place, so a reader can follow the analysis without parsing the code or piecing the rationale together from across the manuscript. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) make such a representation practical: LLMs now translate natural-language descriptions into executable code with considerable reliability [@jiang2026survey; @shah_automating_2026; @chen2021codex; @lai_ds1000_2023; @huang_executionbased_2022], so once a decision is described in a schema, an LLM can generate and validate the corresponding code directly from it. The same representation also makes extending an analysis easier. Data analysis is often underdetermined, with many plausible choices regarding data preprocessing, transformation, aggregation, and model specification [@gao_nonstandard_2026; @bertran_many_2026; @luo_can_2025], and a reader may reasonably want to know whether a conclusion would still hold under one of these other choices, for example, "What if we had included observations with $x \leq 0$?" This question motivates multiverse analysis [@steegen2016] and specification curve analysis [@simonsohn2020], which report a result across the set of defensible analytical choices rather than a single path through it. Because each decision is recorded explicitly rather than embedded in code, a reader can specify such an alternative directly and have it evaluated through the same schema and the same LLM-based translation into code, rather than modifying the original script by hand. -->

In this paper, we present a schema designed to describe data analysis [in a structured way that captures the decisions and their rationale, as well as the inputs and outputs of each step]. We also demonstrate how this schema, coupled with large language models (LLMs), can be used to generate code scripts from natural-language descriptions in manuscripts, and explore alternative decision choices. We present two applications. The first takes the perspective of an author supplying a schema alongside a published manuscript, using the GAITD regression analysis of heaped smoking data in @yee2025heaping. A reader can then specify an alternative file, coupled with the original schema, to compare model performance under a different inflation-alteration specification. The second, the many-analysts football study, considers the opposite situation, where no schema is supplied and the workflow serves instead as a reproducibility test. It extracts a schema from a simplified version of each team's report, generates and validates the corresponding code, and compares the result against that team's published estimate. This comparison also uncovers an inconsistency in one team's published report between the covariate described in the text and the one implied by their results. We further demonstrate how the schema supports specification and exploration of three alternative random effect structures for Team 5.

The paper is organized as follows: In @sec-method, we present our methodology, including the schema representation for describing data analysis, the specification of the alternative file, and the workflow for generating and validating code from the schema with LLMs. In @sec-gaitd, we construct a schema for a published GAITD regression analysis and show how it allows a reader to evaluate an alternative specification directly. In @sec-application, we apply the workflow as a reproducibility test to the many-analysts football study, recovering the reported results for most teams and discussing the failed cases. Finally, in @sec-discussion, we discuss the implications of our work and potential future directions.

The reproducibility movement has been a major development in modern scientific research, motivated in part by concerns regarding the replication of published findings and the increasing reliance on computational methods across disciplines. Reproducibility concerns whether a result can be regenerated given the data, code, and computational environment, whereas comprehension concerns whether the audience can reconstruct the analytical decisions made by the authors, understand the rationale behind those decisions, and confidently modify the code to explore alternative choices. # Methodology {#sec-method}

## A schema for describing data analysis {#sec-schema}

We represent a data analysis, $\mathcal{S} = \{A_1, A_2, \cdots, A_n\}$, as a sequence of $n$ analysis decisions $A_i$, applied to a dataset $\mathcal{D}$, where each step, $A_i$, is defined as a tuple:

\begin{equation}
A_{i} = \langle f_{i}, \pi_{i}, \rho_{i}, \mathcal{I}_{i}, \mathcal{O}_{i}, \omega_{i} \rangle.
\end{equation}


$f_{i} \in \mathcal{F}$ is the *objective* of a step, identifying the problem the *decision*, $\pi_{i} \in \Pi$, is trying to solve. $\rho_{i}$ is the *rationale* provided for choosing the decision $\pi_{i}$. All of the three fields are written in short natural language sentences, and together they form a self-contained account of each decision in the analysis. As an example, @lst-schema presents the schema that describes the steps for calculating the Human Development Index (HDI) [@hdi]:

  1) Scale all four variables (life expectancy, expected years of schooling, mean years of schooling, and GNI per capita) to the [0, 1] range.
  2) Combine the two education variables (expected years of schooling and mean years of schooling) into a single education variable.
  3) Combine the three dimensions (health, education, and income) into a single index using a geometric mean. 

:::{#lst-schema lst-cap="An example schema for calculating Human Development Index (HDI)"}
````yaml
meta:
  type: schema
nodes:
- id: step-scaling
  objective: how to handle variables in different scales?
  decision: apply min-max scaling to each variable
  rationale: to convert the variables to the same scale for future
    construction of a single index
- id: step-education
  objective: how to combine the two education-related variables?
  decision: take the average
  rationale: the arithmetic mean allows perfect substitutability
    between the two variables
- id: step-combine
  objective: how to combine the three dimensions into a single index?
  decision: use the geometric mean
  rationale: the geometric mean penalizes uneven development 
    among the three core dimensions
````
:::

In the file, the `meta` field at the top marks the document as a schema (`type: schema`), and `nodes` below it records the analysis as a list of steps. Each step carries an `id` that names it, together with the `objective`, `decision`, and `rationale` fields holding $f_i$, $\pi_i$, and $\rho_i$. As an example, the objective of step 3 is to combine the three dimensions to create a single index. The geometric mean (the decision) is chosen over a simple arithmetic mean (an alternative - introduced in @sec-alternative) because it penalizes uneven development among the three dimensions (the rationale). 

 Where a dataset $\mathcal{D}$ is available, $\mathcal{I}_i$ and $\mathcal{O}_i$ record this mapping as part of the schema, so that it is fixed in advance rather than inferred at the point of code generation. Because the schema specifies an analysis before its code exists, $\mathcal{O}_i$ may name a variable that is not yet in the dataset. In contrast, $\mathcal{I}_i$ must already be in scope, comprising variables in the original dataset together with the outputs of all previous steps:

$$\mathcal{I}_{i} \subseteq \left( \mathcal{D} \cup \bigcup_{j < i} \mathcal{O}_{j} \right), \quad \forall i \in \{2, \dots, n\}.$$

<!-- In practice it most often names a new column added to the evolving dataset through non-standard evaluation, as in `tidyverse`-style pipelines. -->

A schema can be written by hand, or drafted by an LLM from an existing description of the analysis, such as the methodology section of a manuscript. In the latter case, $\mathcal{I}_i$ and $\mathcal{O}_i$ are inferred by the model whenever a dataset is provided, and each step carries a categorical confidence score, $\omega_{i}$ (low, medium, high), defined as the model's confidence that the recorded $(f_i, \pi_i, \rho_i)$ correctly reflects the source text. 

## Describing alternatives {#sec-alternative}

Recording a step's decision $\pi_i$ does not mean it is the only one that could satisfy its objective $f_i$: a reader may want to revisit the decision made for some of these steps and consider alternatives that address the same objective, the premise of multiverse analysis [@steegen2016; @simonsohn2020]. Formally, a step in the schema can have a candidate set of alternatives: step $i$ may admit $k_i$ decisions that all satisfy its objective $f_i$, $\{A_i^1, \dots, A_i^{k_i}\}$, of which the decision $\pi_i$ recorded in the schema is just one member, $A_i^1$. An alternative file specifies the remaining candidates, $A_i^2, \dots, A_i^{k_i}$, for a subset of steps $C \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$. 

The overall structure of an alternative file is shown in @lst-alternatives-skeleton. The `meta` field at the top identifies the file as an alternative specification (`type: alternatives`), and the file-level `branch` field, either `single` or `multi`, determines how the candidates at each step are combined. The `nodes` field then holds one entry for every step in $C$. Each entry uses `overrides` to name the step it applies to in the original schema, then lists that step's alternative decisions and their rationale.

:::{#lst-alternatives-skeleton lst-cap="The skeleton of an alternative YAML file, which consists of a `branch` mode and a list of covered steps."}
````yaml
meta:
  type: alternatives
  branch: single | multi
nodes:
  - overrides: <step id>
    alternatives:
      - id: <alternative id>
        decision: <...>
        rationale: <...>
      - id: <alternative id>
        ...
  - overrides: <step id>
    alternatives:
      ...
  ...
````
:::

Under `branch: single`, every step is restricted to a single candidate decision. These alternatives, together with the rest of the original schema, form one new analysis. This is useful when an analyst already has a specific alternative analysis in mind and wants to evaluate it as a whole. @lst-alternatives-single fills in the skeleton to construct an alternative HDI pipeline construction, using a harmonic mean to combine the two education variables in Step 2 and an arithmetic mean to combine the three dimensions in Step 3.

:::{#lst-alternatives-single lst-cap="A sample alternative file that changes the decisions for Step 2 and Step 3 in calculating Human Development Index (HDI)."}
````yaml
meta:
  type: alternatives
  branch: single
nodes:
  - overrides: step-education
    alternatives:
      - id: harmonic-mean
        decision: take the harmonic mean of the two education variables
        rationale: penalizes disparity between the two schooling measures
          rather than allowing one to compensate for the other
  - overrides: step-combine
    alternatives:
      - id: arith-mean
        decision: use an arithmetic mean
        rationale: a simple average of the three dimensions
````
:::

Sometimes a reader, instead, wants to test a range of alternatives for one or more steps independently. Under `branch: multi`, each covered step may take any of its alternatives or keep its original decision, and every such combination across steps becomes a separate analysis. In @lst-alternatives-multi, one alternative is specified for the education step and two for the combination step. Together with the original schema, this produces $(1+1) \times (2+1) = 6$ analyses. More generally, with $k_i$ candidates at each step $i \in C$, crossing all candidates yields $\prod_{i \in C} k_i$ analyses.
  
:::{#lst-alternatives-multi lst-cap="A sample alternative file that explores one alternative decision for Step 2 and two for Step 3 in calculating Human Development Index (HDI). Combining these alternatives with the original schema produces a total of six (1+1) × (2+1) = 6 analyses."}
````yaml
meta:
  type: alternatives
  branch: multi
nodes:
  - overrides: step-education
    alternatives:
      - id: harmonic-mean
        decision: take the harmonic mean of the two education variables
        rationale: penalizes disparity between the two schooling measures
          rather than allowing one to compensate for the other
  - overrides: step-combine
    alternatives:
      - id: arith-mean
        decision: use an arithmetic mean
        rationale: a simple average of the three dimensions
      - id: min-agg
        decision: use the minimum of the three dimensions
        rationale: a "weakest-link" aggregation that penalizes any single
          lagging dimension more strongly than an average would
````
:::

Existing multiverse tooling, such as the `multiverse` package in R [@sarma2023], expresses each branch in code, while our alternatives are instead specified at the level of decisions, in natural language, from which modern LLMs can generate the corresponding code. Keeping them in a separate file also changes who can pose the alternative question: a multiverse is conventionally built by the original analyst exploring their own garden of forking paths, whereas an alternative file can be written by a reader after reading the published manuscript, against a schema the author has already supplied, to investigate questions that interest them. 

## Workflow {#sec-workflow}

The reliability of the generated code depends primarily on the quality of the schema. A schema that faithfully records the decisions of an analysis, in the form set out in @sec-schema, leaves little to be interpreted at the code generation stage, since the objective and the decision at each step are stated explicitly. The errors that remain are in the code implementation rather than the analysis: a missing `library()` call, or a misnamed function argument.

The validation stage is designed to resolve errors of this kind. The validation agent executes the script in a sandbox environment and, when execution fails, receives the script together with the error message and the line number at which it occurred, and returns a revised script. The revised script is then executed again, and the cycle continues until the script completes without error, a maximum number of attempts is reached, or the user terminates the process. Application to the many-analysts football study in @sec-application shows that this procedure resolves most of the syntax errors that arise in data wrangling and statistical modelling.

The same generation-validation procedure applies to multiple analyses. When a schema is augmented with an alternative file, the expansion described in @sec-alternative produces one schema for each combination of decisions, and each resulting schema is passed through the same generation and validation procedure independently.
 
@fig-workflow gives an overview of the workflow, which provides two paths for using a schema. Passing a schema through the code generation and validation stages produces a script whose execution yields the estimates of the analysis, which can be compared with the estimates originally reported, serving as a reproducibility check. A schema can also be augmented with an alternative file, expanding it into a multiverse of parallel analyses, so that the author and subsequent readers can explore the  reported result under different decisions. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-workflow
#| out.width: 100%
#| echo: false
#| fig.cap: "Overview of the schema-driven analysis workflow. Schemas can be authored manually or generated from natural language manuscripts by an LLM. Schemas are used to generate code, which is validated through iterative execution in a sandboxed environment and repaired when errors occur. Alternative specifications can expand a schema into a multiverse of parallel analyses."
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figures/workflow.png"))
```

We now analyze the uncertainty of the pipeline itself: for a step $k$ extracted by a model $M$ from a source text $T$, we decompose the total uncertainty of the pipeline at that step into a specification term and an implementation term,

$$V_k^{\text{total}}(M) = V_k^{\text{spec}}(M) + V_k^{\text{impl}}(M),$$

where each component is defined as the expected pairwise divergence, $d(\cdot, \cdot) \in [0, 1]$, between independent runs at the corresponding stage. Specifically, $V_k^{\text{spec}}(M)$ measures variation across repeated schema extractions from $T$ and $V_k^{\text{impl}}(M)$ measures variation across repeated code generations from a single fixed schema. We can further decompose the specification term into an epistemic and an aleatoric component [@kendall2017; @hullermeier2021]:

$$V_k^{\text{spec}}(M) = V_k^{\text{epistemic}}(M) + V_k^{\text{aleatoric}},$$

The epistemic component, $V_k^{\text{epistemic}}(M)$, reflects when the model fails to recover a decision that is unambiguously specified in  $T$. The aleatoric component, $V_k^{\text{aleatoric}}$, captures the uncertainty in the source itself: the text $T$ is unclear at step $k$, independent of $M$. This distinction has a direct diagnostic use in the quality of the data anlaysis. Persistent dispersion across increasingly capable models suggests that the observed variation reflects ambiguity in the source since a more capable model cannot recover the authors' intent that is not sufficiently expressed in the source text.

# Application: GAITD regression of heaped smoking data {#sec-gaitd}

In this section we demonstrate the workflow in the case where an author provides a faithful schema alongside a published manuscript, which a reader can then use to question and explore the analysis, following the second path in @fig-workflow. We use @yee2025heaping's GAITD regression analysis of heaped smoking data, published in the Annals of Applied Statistics, as the example. @yee2025heaping report four separate smoking-related responses, and for demonstration purposes, we build the schema for only the first response, smoking initiation age (P1, Section 5.1 of their paper). The same workflow extends to the other three cases.

The schema in @lst-heaping comprises fourteen entries, each recording an *objective*, a *decision*, and a *rationale* in the structure introduced in @sec-schema. Consider `special_value_mid_risk`: the decision is to treat ages 12-14 and 19-21 as one inflated group with extra probability mass, since these ages show a moderate, secondary peak in the spikeplots with the high-risk group (ages 15-18) showing the most prominent peak. Recording the rationale along with the decision allows a reader to agree or disagree with the authors' choice, and to question and explore the analysis, as we do later in this section.

:::{#lst-heaping lst-cap="A schema for the GAITD regression analysis of smoking initiation age in @yee2025heaping, constructed from the manuscript and intended to be provided alongside it as a self-contained account of the analysis."}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat("````yaml\n")
cat(readLines(here::here("schemas/schema_draft.yaml")), sep = "\n")
cat("````\n")
```
:::

Assembling the schema does not require additional analysis from the authors, but to collect the decisions and rationale existing in the manuscript and supplementary material. 


<!-- required no analysis the authors had not already done, but it did require collecting the decisions from two documents and, in places, from code alone. Five of the fourteen appear nowhere in the manuscript. The manuscript records that cases with missing values in the adjustment variables were deleted and that the sample was restricted to respondents under 80; it does not record that `TC30`, `TCquit`, and `SCA` are exempt from that completeness check, that `SCA` and `SIA` are set to missing wherever `SCA - SIA < 0`, that marital status and education are overwritten by age for respondents under 20, or the two-branch rule that defines the ever-smoker sample. Each of these survives only as executable code in the supplementary material, and their stated rationale, where there is one, is a code comment: the completeness exemption is explained by the remarks that the variables are "interlaced with NAs" and that a missing value "means not yet quit, which is okay", the ever-smoker rule by the comment "Complex to handle NAs", and the data-quality correction by the single word "Bad". The two recodings carry no comment at all; a reader must infer their purpose from a note several pages later, written for another purpose, observing that marital status, education, and smoking initiation age "were not measured in those aged 19 or less". Recovering these decisions is exactly the piecing-together the schema is meant to remove, and it is worth emphasising that @yee2025heaping's supplementary material is unusually thorough as it walks through the analysis in a tutorial style, states general modelling guidelines upfront, and discusses competing options it rejected.  -->

As a check that this schema is accurate, generating and validating code from it produces the R script in @lst-script-sia, which reproduces the coefficients reported in Table 2 of @yee2025heaping. Since the code was generated without access to the manuscript or the authors' script, the match shows that the schema records everything needed to reproduce the analysis. A schema of this kind could therefore accompany a manuscript as reproducibility material in its own right, alongside code and data, and a reader can rely on it as an accurate account of the analysis it documents.

:::{#lst-script-sia lst-cap="The R script generated and validated from the schema in @lst-heaping, annotated with the `id` of the schema step each block implements."}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat("````r\n")
cat(readLines(here::here("schemas/script_iter1_annotated.R")), sep = "\n")
cat("````\n")
```
:::

@yee2025heaping's supplementary material reports an investigation from a reviewer, who suggested splitting the mid-risk group into two, keeping ages 12-14 as inflated but treating ages 19-21 as altered instead, since that older subgroup shows a qualitatively different, declining pattern of uptake. @lst-ap1921 encodes the reviewer's suggestion as an alternative file, overriding three steps at once: `special_value_mid_risk` narrows the inflated group to ages 12-14, `alteration_operator_decision` turns on an alteration group for ages 19-21, and `covariate_selection` drops to an intercept-only model, matching how the authors themselves computed AIC for this comparison; `branch: single` ties the three overrides into one refit, rather than crossing them into separate branches. Generating and validating code from this alternative file reproduces the AIC of 19,340.4 that @yee2025heaping reports. Here the question was answered because the authors chose to report the refit in their supplement; with the schema available, any reader who raises such a question can answer it directly. 

:::{#lst-ap1921 lst-cap="An alternative YAML file specifying a joint change to the mid-risk inflation, alteration, and covariate steps in the GAITD schema, treating ages 19-21 as an alteration group rather than pooling them into the mid-risk inflated group."}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat("````yaml\n")
cat(readLines(here::here("schemas/alt_ap1921.yaml")), sep = "\n")
cat("````\n")
```
:::




# Application: many-analysts football study {#sec-application}

@sec-gaitd assumed an author willing to supply a schema. Most published analyses come with no such thing, so we now ask what the same workflow is worth when none exists. Applied to a manuscript alone, it becomes a reproducibility test: extract a schema from what the paper says, generate and validate code from it, and compare the result against what the paper reports. Agreement means the description was sufficient to regenerate the result. Disagreement means something is missing, ambiguous, or wrong, and is the more informative outcome. We apply this to the many-analysts football study of @silberzahn2018, which gives 29 independent descriptions of an analysis of one dataset, each with a reported effect size to test against.

@silberzahn2018 invited 29 research groups to conduct the same data analysis, answering whether referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skin-toned players than to light-skin-toned players. The provided dataset contains two raters' skin color ratings of players' pictures, the aggregated number of red cards received by a player from a referee across all matches in that player-referee pair, and other relevant player, referee, and game characteristics: player birthday, height, weight, player position, league country, number of victories, ties, and defeats, and number of yellow and red cards received. In @silberzahn2018, each group first conducted an initial analysis separately, followed by a round-robin peer evaluation. Each group was then given the opportunity to incorporate feedback from the discussion and submitted a final analysis as a report with a formal Method section. All the materials related to the study are publicly available on the Open Science Framework (OSF).

Based on the reports presented by each team, most participating groups adopted a modelling approach to estimate the effect of skin color rating on the likelihood of receiving a red card. As an illustrative example, Team 5 first transformed the data into player–game observations, resulting in a binary response variable for whether a player received a red card, and removed observations with missing values using list-wise deletion. The resulting data were modelled using a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with a binomial error distribution. The average skin color rating from two raters was used as the primary covariate, and its estimated coefficient was the main parameter of interest. To account for unobserved heterogeneity, the model included random effects for player and referee, as well as the average skin color rating across referee's country of origin. While Team 5's analysis illustrates one possible approach, other teams may adopt different data preprocessing decisions, distributional assumptions (e.g., linear, logistic, or Poisson models), or specifications of fixed and random effects, or may conduct the analysis in a Bayesian framework.

Team reports are not straightforward to use as input directly. Beyond the analysis of interest, whether skin color rating predicts red cards, the many-analysts study also includes a second research question and report confidence interval calculations for the estimated effect, neither of which is relevant to the schema extraction or code generation we study here. The report structure adds a further complication: some teams write the final analysis as edits against the initial analysis, for example a covariate dropped, a variable rescaled, a different outcome, rather than as a self-contained methodology section. Recovering a single, self-contained methodology description while setting aside the unrelated research question is its own nontrivial comprehension problem, separate from the task of generating the schema and analysis code that we study here. We therefore pre-extract a simplified methodology text for each team and use this, rather than the original report, as the input for our experiment. The Appendix follows one team through the whole pipeline, giving the pre-extracted text, the schema extracted from it, and the code generated from that schema, along with the prompts used at each stage. 

Each team's text is then passed through the workflow of @sec-method unchanged: schema extraction, code generation, and validation.

To accelerate the evaluation of each script, we manually replace, in place, the `lm()`/`glm()` command with `fixest::feols()`/`fixest::feglm()` [@fixest] for generalized linear models, and the `lme4::glmer()` [@lme4] function with `glmmTMB::glmmTMB()` [@glmmTMB-1] for generalized mixed-effects models, after the scripts are generated but before validation. These two functions are in-place replacements of the standard functions for estimating the relevant models, with multi-threading in C++ [@fixest] and Template Model Builder (TMB) [@glmmTMB-2] for better performance. This replacement should not affect the estimation of the effect size. All LLM-related runs are conducted with Claude Opus 4.5.

```{r}
#| echo: false
# df <- read_csv(here::here("data/res.csv"))
# df |> count(validate_iter_n) |> knitr::kable()
```

Of the 29 teams, we report results for 25. The remaining four (Teams 7, 12, 17, and 18) specify analyses that are too computationally expensive to run inside an iterative validate-and-repair loop, regardless of whether the schema or generated code is correct: Teams 17 and 18 both specify MCMC-based hierarchical models with thousands of random effects, Team 7 a Dirichlet process profile regression, and Team 12 a zero-inflated Poisson regression with several thousand fixed-effect parameters. Across the 25 teams we reproduce, all team scripts were successfully executed after the validation phase. Notably, two scripts ran successfully without any validation, whereas the vast majority reached completion after two or three iterations. The most frequent correction involved resolving broken and overflowing syntax in comments. 

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-res-schema
#| out.width: 90%
#| out.height: 80%
#| fig.cap: "Comparison of the odds ratio of the effect of skin color on receiving red cards in football games from our schema-based reproduction (reproduced) vs. the effect size reported in @silberzahn2018 (reported). Teams are ordered by the absolute difference between the reproduced and reported odds ratio. The reproduction recovers the reported odds ratio closely for most teams; the largest deviations occur for Team 1, 9, 15, 21, 23, and 27."
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figures/res-schema.png"))
```

@fig-res-schema shows the comparison of the estimated effect sizes, in odds ratio, from our workflow (reproduced) and those reported in @silberzahn2018 (reported). The odds ratio is well recovered for most teams, though six show a noticeably larger gap: Team 1, 9, 15, 21, 23, and 27. Each of these is worth examining, and the schema is what makes the examination possible: because the extracted decisions can be inspected before any code is written, a discrepancy can be attributed to the report, to the code generated from it, or to neither.

Two of the six are properties of the report rather than of our pipeline. Team 9 is the clearest: the text names "referee country" as the covariate, while the reported estimation table lists "player country". The report contradicts itself, and no reading of the manuscript can settle which model produced the published estimate. Team 27 is ambiguous rather than contradictory. The authors write: "In addition to the independent variables specified in the initial approach, ... a variable for player position was included, as well as a variable for the league of the player." A statistician might reasonably read this as shorthand for extending the model with interactions, consistent with how the other covariates entered the initial model; read literally, it adds only main effects. The schema records what the text says in both cases, and the discrepancy that follows is the test's finding, not its failure: these are the two reports whose description of the analysis is not sufficient to regenerate the result.

The confidence score $\omega_i$ separates these two cases in a way worth noting. For Team 27, extraction returned `create_interaction_terms` with medium confidence, flagging the step whose reading is in doubt before any code was written. For Team 9, every step came back with high confidence, which is the correct response rather than an oversight: the report's text is unambiguous on its own terms, and the inconsistency appears only when that text is set against the estimation table. Since $\omega_i$ records the model's confidence that the schema reflects the source text, it can surface a description that is ambiguous, but not one that is internally clear and contradicted elsewhere. Catching the latter requires comparing the schema against the reported results, which is what the test as a whole does.

Teams 1 and 23 are failures of a different kind, and they are ours: the schema is right and the code is wrong. Both require reshaping the data from player-referee pairs to individual games, disaggregating win/loss/draw counts into game-level records. The schema correctly specifies this step, but the generated code fails to execute it as intended, and the resulting error passes through validation silently rather than triggering a repair.

Team 15's discrepancy is unrelated to either stage: it comes down to a difference in default contrast coding between R (our reproduction) and SPSS (the original analysis) — SPSS's effect coding compares each level to the grand mean, while R's default dummy coding compares to a reference level. Setting the `contrast` option in R to match recovers the reported odds ratio exactly, so this reflects a software convention rather than a modeling or LLM error.

That leaves Team 21, whose discrepancy we have been unable to explain. Examining both the extracted schema and the generated code turned up nothing that accounts for the gap, and we report it as unresolved rather than assign it to a cause we cannot establish; the procedure localizes most discrepancies, but evidently not all of them. Setting Team 21 aside, the five remaining discrepancies divide into two whose reports cannot be resolved to a single analysis, two where our code generation failed, and one that reflects a difference in software convention. Only the middle pair are errors in the workflow itself; the first two are what the test was built to surface.

## Exploring alternatives

During the modelling process, researchers may consider a range of alternative specifications, such as different covariate and random effects structures, before arriving at a final model. This can be seen as a set of alternative decisions within the same modelling step, which fits naturally into the schema workflow described in @sec-alternative. As an example, we return to Team 5, whose analysis was described above. Having settled on a binomial GLMM with a logit link for the probability that a player receives a red card in a single game, Team 5 tests three random effect structures:

\begin{align*}
\textbf{Model 1 (gm1):} \quad \text{logit}(p_{ijk}) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{ijk} + u_{j} + v_{k} \\
u_{j} &\sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{player}}), \quad v_{k} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{ref}}) \\[1.5em]
\textbf{Model 2 (gm2):} \quad \text{logit}(p_{ijk}) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{ijk} + u_{j} + v_{0k} + v_{1k} X_{ijk} \\
u_{j} &\sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{player}}), \quad \mathbf{v}_{k} \sim N\left(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{ref}}\right) \\[1.5em]
\textbf{Model 3 (gm3):} \quad \text{logit}(p_{ijkm}) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{ijkm} + u_{j} + v_{k} + w_{0m} + w_{1m} X_{ijkm} \\
u_{j} &\sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{player}}), \quad v_{k} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{ref}}), \quad \mathbf{w}_{m} \sim N\left(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{country}}\right)
\end{align*}

where $p$ denotes the probability of a player receiving a red card, and $X$ represents the player's skin tone rating. The subscripts $i, j, k,$ and $m$ index the individual observation, player, referee, and the referee's home country, respectively. The parameter $\beta_0$ represents the global baseline log-odds of receiving a red card, and $\beta_1$ estimates the fixed effect of a player's skin tone. The random effects include

  * a random intercept for players, $u_j \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{player}})$, in Models 1, 2, and 3,
  * a random intercept for referees, $v_k \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\text{ref}})$, in Models 1 and 3, plus an additional random slope for referees in Model 2, and
  * a random intercept and slope for referee countries, $\mathbf{w}_{m} \sim N\left(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{country}}\right)$, in Model 3.

All three are specified in a single YAML file, following the format described in @sec-alternative and shown in @lst-yaml-alternative. Merging it with Team 5's schema produces one schema per alternative, and each is passed through the same code generation and validation used for the original, yielding three validated scripts from one file and no hand-editing of the team's code. The estimated effect of skin tone is unchanged across this expansion, matching the value Team 5 report and shown for this team in @fig-res-schema.


:::{#lst-yaml-alternative lst-cap="Example of a YAML file specifying alternatives for the random effects structure in the many-analysts analysis of Team 5."}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat("````yaml\n")
cat(readLines(here::here("schemas/football-grp5-alt.yaml")), sep = "\n")
cat("````\n")
```
:::

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

Our results highlight a persistent gap between computational reproducibility and analytical understandability in modern data analysis workflows. Current reproducibility practices ensure that published results can be regenerated from shared data and code, but as analyses grow in complexity and involve iterative decision-making, they fall well short of making those analyses understandable to readers. Our proposed schema addresses this gap by introducing an intermediate representation that explicitly encodes analytical decisions to bridge between narrative descriptions and implementation details. When coupled with LLMs, this representation enables the extraction of analytical structure from written reports, its translation into analysis scripts, and the exploration of alternative analytical choices.

Our approach differs in this respect from recent work that builds fully automated systems using multiple LLM agents to plan, generate, execute, and refine data analyses [@jansen2025; @hu_automated_2024]. These systems rely on the same underlying capability of translating analytical specifications into code that our workflow uses, but they aim to automate the analytical decisions themselves, not just their translation into code. The failure modes we document in @sec-application suggest this is premature: even the comparatively narrower task of translating an already-specified decision into working code is not yet fully reliable. We take this as support for our position that the harder and more consequential part of a data analysis is the sequence of decisions a researcher makes, not the code that implements them, and that this part should remain explicit and in the hands of the analyst rather than be automated away.

Where no schema is supplied, the same workflow serves as a reproducibility test, and we apply it in this form to the many-analysts football study. It surfaces inconsistencies and ambiguities in the original reports that computational reproducibility alone would not catch: Team 9's report names one covariate in its text and a different one in its estimation table, a contradiction that is invisible if one only re-runs the authors' code, and that only becomes apparent once the described analysis is written down as an explicit set of decisions and executed. Examining the largest discrepancies also separates defects in the reports from failures of our own pipeline — two of each, with a fifth attributable to a difference in software convention. The separation is possible because the schema sits between the manuscript and the code and can be checked against the manuscript on its own, and it matters for where effort should be directed: an unresolvable report calls for disambiguation at the source, and the confidence score $\omega_i$ is the natural hook for it, having flagged the disputed step in Team 27's report before any code was written, whereas a code-generation failure calls for improvements to the validation stage itself.

A caveat applies to the failure modes we report: they describe the behaviour of one model at one point in time. Current models parse methodology text reliably for the most part, and where they slip is on statistical nuance that a trained reader supplies without thinking. The phrase "a random effect of referee number across average rating" would be read by most statisticians as implying both a random intercept and a random slope; read literally, as the model reads it, it specifies a random slope only. This points to a gap between current models and human analysts in specialized statistical knowledge [@sun_lambda_2026], but given the pace at which these models are improving we expect this particular gap to narrow, and we do not regard it as a structural limitation of the workflow. What the workflow provides, independently of model capability, is somewhere to catch such a misreading: the schema is inspectable before any code is generated, so a misread decision is visible to the analyst as a sentence rather than buried in a script.

Our validate-and-repair loop assumes each candidate script can be executed and diagnosed within an interactive timeframe. This assumption does not hold for analyses that are too computationally expensive to run inside such a loop (Teams 7, 12, 17, and 18 in the many-analysts football study). As a future direction, this could be addressed by implementing a background job queue to allow longer-running scripts to be executed asynchronously.

Turning to the other stage, the validation loop successfully corrects a range of implementation issues, including errors caused by overflowing comments and other syntax problems. What it does not catch are transformations that run without error but do not do what the schema asked, of which the reshaping failures behind Teams 1 and 23 are the clearest instance: changing the unit of analysis from player-referee dyads to individual games produces code that executes and returns an estimate regardless of whether the disaggregation was done correctly. We also observe some difficulties in parsing birthdates. Since the LLM does not have access to the underlying raw data, due to privacy constraints, it must rely on trial and error when inferring the correct date format, in this case "DD-MM-YYYY". This suggests that certain types of data analysis tasks may not be fully automatable in settings where the model cannot directly inspect the data, even if the data is theoretically available for computation.

While the schema requires a rationale $\rho_i$ for each decision, nothing in the format itself can guarantee that this rationale is substantive rather than perfunctory; an analyst can satisfy the schema with a low-effort entry in the same way that a required code comment or commit message can be filled with boilerplate. The schema makes recording a decision's rationale cheap and structured, but, as with any documentation requirement, cannot enforce that authors use it thoughtfully. It remains an open question whether resolving $\mathcal{I}_i$ and $\mathcal{O}_i$ to concrete dataset variables ahead of time, rather than leaving this mapping for the LLM to infer at the point of code generation, meaningfully improves the reliability of the resulting code.

The reproducibility-understandability issue considered in this work is still at an early stage, and some software design choices are worth examining. We currently implement a prototype as an R package, although the understandability problem is broadly applicable to statistical analyses and is not associated with any particular programming language. Hence, we envision the implementation eventually evolving into a general purpose tool, such as a command-line utility, that can support analyses across different programming languages. In the current implementation, analytical decisions are recorded in a single YAML file. An alternative would be to record individual decisions in separate Markdown files. While YAML files provide an explicit structure for machine readability, Markdown files offer greater flexibility for documenting decisions. Recording decisions in separate files would also allow them to be linked across time, showing how decisions evolve over the course of an analysis. This could in turn support a broader research-management system, provided that decisions are properly attributed to individual researchers and that a record of the changes leading to the final analysis is maintained.
